summary:
[Fair warning: the soundtrack is a little too excited to meet you!]

We wanted to explore what happens when we try to build something that can reach out of the earth's orbit. What should it carry? Where should it go? And what happens when a seemingly perfectly choice makes several other things harder?

We developed a mission design game combining an interactive visual novel with a spacecraft workshop and simulator. Players begin with a problem to investigate, discuss possible designs with the characters, check their resources, and build a spacecraft they can test. Adding another instrument changes a lot more than its scientific possibilities: it also changes mass, power demand, cost and the amount of data that needs to reach Earth.

The game addresses the challenge by letting players follow those connections through a complete design experiment. Its explanations draw on NASA resources, while its models simplify the engineering for learning. We wanted people to have somewhere to work through the confusing questions, including the ones they only discover after their first design doesn’t work as expected, simply by mistake.
details:
The part of space mission design that interested us was how quickly one question can become super complicated. Suppose we want observations after sunset. We choose a thermal camera. Then we need to power it, store its observations and send them back to Earth. Now, choosing the camera means considering batteries, communications and orbit too. It becomes difficult to know which decision to make first.

The game opens with a historical quote about flight, then come up five mission stories. In “After the Smoke,” the player considers a mission that needs thermal observations after sunset. The characters discuss why those observations matter before beginning with hardware. We wanted the story to give our decisions a reason, with room for curiosity and some humor!

As the mission continues, players can compare designs and check their resources. It is tempting to add another instrument because it could collect something useful. But the extra capability brings demands of its own. The player has to consider whether the rest of the spacecraft can support that choice.

The workshop has 77 parts and 91 recipes! Build cards connect the story’s proposed designs to spacecraft that can be assembled. Players can combine parts into modules, save their creation and take it into the simulator.

This connection is also one of the difficult coding problems. In the workshop, a spacecraft can contain modules made from other modules. The simulator needs to understand the ingredients inside that assembly to calculate its behavior. Otherwise, the player could carefully choose a battery or instrument and then discover that their choice makes no difference during testing! The link between construction and simulation is essential to what we wanted the game to do.

Another challenge is deciding how much information to show at once. Space already feels overwhelming. Putting everything on one screen makes it so much harder to understand the relationships between them. We have tried to organize the experience around the questions the player is currently trying to answer, with guidance available along the way. The workshop and simulator also remain independently accessible, so players can experiment without following a story.

The simulation gives those experiments consequences. In one demonstration, the spacecraft’s battery stayed above 88% charge, yet it lost a large amount of data when its storage buffer overflowed. That is an interesting place to get stuck: the power system looks healthy, but the observations still aren’t reaching the ground. Now there is a better question to check. Should we collect less data, change the payload, or reconsider the radio?

We developed the game in Godot, using GDScript with pixel-art environments and character portraits. A lot of assets were downloaded from the internet, from itch.io. NASA’s Systems Engineering Handbook, small-spacecraft technology resources and orbital references support the explanations and model context. Component prices and ratings are simplified teaching values.

We hope players become more comfortable working through an uncertain design. They can have an idea, build it, discover something they overlooked and try another version. Being able to follow that “what if?” is what excites us about the project.
